title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
gist: A magistrate judge ordered Meta to identify the executives and staff who authorized torrenting of shadow libraries to train AI, rejecting its claim that no one made a decision. The order also compels server command-history logs that could show whether Meta seeded pirated works.

themes.theme: Discovery order on Meta torrenting decisions

insights.claim: Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely ordered Meta to identify everyone who made, authorized or approved decisions to obtain shadow library datasets, rejecting its narrower reading of 'decision' and 'identify'.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Discovery is moving up the chain of command and could put executive conduct, not just engineers, at issue.
insights.quote: Not buying Meta’s arguments, Hixon said that authors did not limit their request to formal decisions

insights.claim: Meta's defense that early Llama dataset acquisition was an 'informal approach' with no one making decisions was rejected, and the judge noted the request covers all decision-makers, not a single one.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Diffuse-responsibility defenses are not holding at the discovery stage.
insights.quote: it asks about all the decision makers

insights.claim: Meta must also answer what happened to pirated works not used for AI training.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This broadens exposure beyond training-data fair use into possession and distribution.

insights.claim: Unsealed messages allegedly show the LibGen download followed 'a prior escalation to MZ' (Mark Zuckerberg), and staff testified that some downloads needed director or VP-level approval, undermining Meta's staff-scapegoat narrative.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Potential CEO involvement raises litigation, settlement and reputational stakes.

insights.claim: Staff pushed back internally, with one saying torrenting from a corporate laptop did not feel right, and leadership allegedly halted then resumed Anna's Archive downloads.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Internal dissent documents help plaintiffs show willfulness.
insights.quote: “torrenting from a corporate laptop doesn’t feel right.”

insights.claim: Plaintiffs argue Meta could not have downloaded 80.6 TB from LibGen and 35.7 TB from Anna's Archive so quickly without also seeding, while Meta says mitigations prevented seeding.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Seeding evidence would turn a data-acquisition case into one about distributing copyrighted works.

insights.claim: The order compels Meta to produce command history files for every server, VM and AWS instance used for torrenting, which could prove seeding and test Meta's mitigation claims.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Logs may supply the closest thing to a smoking gun, raising damages risk for AI-training data practices across the industry.

insights.claim: Under contributory infringement, authors need only prove that Meta facilitated transfers of their works.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The lower bar for contributory claims makes seeding evidence potentially decisive.
